claims.text: The applicable material is equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a homogeneous, single-phase FCC or similar simple solid-solution state.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and yield strength.
The alloy deforms primarily by planar dislocation glide.
Conventional forest hardening does not effectively impede dislocation glide in the alloy.
Ti introduces local lattice distortions into equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The Ti-associated lattice distortions do not provide enough heterogeneous obstacles to cause substantial dislocation pile-up.
The Ti-associated lattice distortions do not provide enough heterogeneous obstacles to activate secondary hardening mechanisms.
Insufficient obstacle strengthening permits dislocations to travel readily along planar slip paths with minimal interactions.
Dynamic recovery limits strain hardening during deformation.
Facile planar glide and limited dislocation interactions lead to low work hardening and thereby to low hardness and yield strength.
Deformation should produce a lower work-hardening rate and less dense or entangled dislocation networks than in alloys containing precipitates or other strong obstacles.
Post-deformation microstructures should exhibit predominantly uniform planar slip, minimal pile-ups, low forest-dislocation density, and little evidence of twinning or dynamic precipitation.
A modification that induces precipitation or other obstacles should produce stronger dislocation impediment than the starting solid solution.

The proposed mechanism is restricted to temperatures and strain rates at which the alloy remains single phase and twinning, phase transformation, and diffusion-controlled deformation do not become dominant.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing stress-strain behavior and in situ TEM/EBSD dislocation evolution in the starting alloy and an obstacle- or precipitation-strengthened modification.

Observation of substantial pile-ups, high forest-dislocation density, twinning, stress-induced precipitation, or work hardening comparable to precipitate-strengthened alloys would falsify the proposed facile-planar-glide explanation.
